name: Antihistamine eye drops

lead: Antihistamine eye drops treat the itching, redness, tearing and eyelid swelling of allergic conjunctivitis, a reaction to pollen, animal dander, dust mites or cosmetics. For people with allergic eyes, calming the reaction can leave the eyes looking whiter and less puffy.

Antihistamines block histamine receptors on the eye surface, and olopatadine and ketotifen also stabilise mast cells. Some combination products pair an antihistamine with a vasoconstrictor such as naphazoline to narrow surface vessels. The evidence in the sources covers allergic eye symptoms and initial comfort of different brands, not general whitening.

paras: Users with seasonal or allergen-triggered symptoms put drops in daily or as symptoms flare. Some are sold over the counter in some countries, and redness only counts as allergic if allergy is the cause.

Drops commonly cause burning or stinging on instillation, and comfort differs between products. Eye care guidance generally treats vasoconstrictor-containing products as unsuitable for long continuous use, since prolonged use can worsen redness. A survey of Australian practitioners found variation in how ocular allergy is managed.

angle.text: For allergic eyes, these drops calm the reaction so itching, redness and lid swelling settle and the eyes look clearer and less puffy. They are studied for allergic conjunctivitis; the effect on non-allergic eyes has not been tested.

lead: Antihistamine eye drops are topical medicines for allergic conjunctivitis, a reaction to allergens such as pollen, animal dander, dust mites or cosmetics that causes itching, redness, tearing and eyelid swelling [1].

Many contemporary products have dual activity, blocking histamine receptors and stabilising mast cells. Olopatadine and ketotifen are named examples, and some are sold over the counter [1][2]. Other products combine an antihistamine such as pheniramine with the vasoconstrictor naphazoline [3].
Published comparisons in the sources address ocular comfort at instillation rather than cosmetic outcomes [2][3].
infobox: Prescription and over the counter, varies by product and country

paras: The main use is symptomatic relief in allergic conjunctivitis. Encyclopedic sources list allergen avoidance, cold compresses and artificial tears for mild disease and antihistamine or dual-action drops for more bothersome symptoms, with corticosteroid drops reserved for severe inflammation under specialist supervision [1].

Red eyes caused by allergy can look unwell, and appearance-focused discussion sometimes mentions these drops for that reason. The research found concerns allergic symptoms and comfort, not whitening of eyes unaffected by allergy.

A 2023 study in minimally symptomatic participants compared initial ocular comfort of 0.7% olopatadine with 0.035% ketotifen fumarate drops [2]. Another 2023 study compared 0.7% olopatadine with a pheniramine maleate and naphazoline hydrochloride combination and reported better initial comfort with olopatadine, suggesting patients might comply better with it [3].
An encyclopedic summary reports that olopatadine was more effective than ketotifen at reducing itching in an antigen challenge model [1].
Eye drops in general can cause burning and stinging, and mast cell stabilisers are described as having fewer side effects than some alternatives [1]. Comfort at instillation varies by product [2][3].

Comfort comparisons of olopatadine against ketotifen and against a naphazoline combination exist [2][3]. A 2025 survey of Australian health practitioners examined knowledge and practice in diagnosing and treating ocular allergy [4]. Registered trials include a phase 2 study of a product in allergic conjunctivitis [5], a trial of a triple-action drop for allergic eye symptoms [6], and a placebo-controlled study of ectoine eye drops and nasal spray [7]. No trials were found evaluating antihistamine drops for cosmetic whitening.
